title: How to write a contractor bid without underpricing the job
dek: Most lost money on a job is lost on the bid. Here are the five lines contractors forget to charge for.
text:
I help run a family framing and contracting business, and the jobs that hurt us most were never the hard ones. They were the ones we bid too low because we priced it in our heads, standing in someone's driveway. 
 A good bid isn't complicated. It just has to include everything the job actually costs. These are the five lines that get missed most. 
 1. Waste and overage 
 You never use exactly what's on the plan. Boards split, cuts go wrong, sheets get damaged. Add a waste percentage to your materials, usually somewhere around 10%, more on jobs with lots of angles or cuts. 
 2. Delivery, dump and disposal fees 
 Lumber delivery, a dumpster, a dump run. These are real costs and they belong on the bid, not in your pocket. 
 3. Drive time and setup 
 If the job is 45 minutes away, that's an hour and a half a day you're paying for. Same with setup and cleanup at the start and end of every day. 
 4. Permits and inspections 
 Permit fees, plan review and the time you spend waiting on an inspector all cost money. Find the fee before you bid, not after you win the job. 
 5. Overhead and profit 
 Insurance, your truck, your phone, your tools, your license. A job has to pay a share of those, plus an actual profit on top. If your bid only covers labor and materials, you're working for free. 
 
  Simple example  
 Materials $4,000 plus 10% waste = $4,400. Labor $3,200. Delivery and dumpster $350. Permit $180. Subtotal $8,130. Then overhead and profit go on top of that, not inside it. 
 
 Put change orders in writing 
 When the homeowner asks for "one more little thing," write it down with a price and get a signature before you do it. Small free extras are how a profitable job turns into a break-even one. 
 We built our own bid and invoice tool so we'd stop guessing numbers on the phone. It's called  Trade Total : one price, no monthly fee, and it opens right on your phone.  Bidding Contractors Pricing

title: How to check if an AI answer is right before you use it
dek: ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini sound sure of themselves even when they're wrong. Here's a 2-minute check I run every time.
text:
I use AI tools every day for work, school and the house. They save me hours. They also hand me wrong answers with total confidence, and the wrong ones look exactly like the right ones. 
 So before I use an AI answer for anything that matters, I run a quick check. It takes about two minutes. 
 Check 1: Is this something that changes? 
 Prices, laws, phone numbers, store hours, who runs a company, what a product costs: these change all the time, and AI tools are often working from old information. If the answer depends on what's true today, look it up on the official site before you trust it. 
 Check 2: Ask where it came from 
 Type: "What is your source for that?" A solid answer points to something you can open and read. A shaky answer gets vague or changes the story. If you can't find the source yourself, treat the answer as a guess. 
 Check 3: Check the numbers by hand 
 AI tools still slip on math, especially with percentages, totals and dates. If the answer has a number you're going to use, a price, a dose, a measurement, a deadline, redo the math on your phone calculator. 
 
  Real example  
 I asked for a materials total on a small job. The list was right. The total was off because one line got counted twice. Thirty seconds with a calculator caught it. 
 
 Check 4: Ask a second way 
 Ask the same question with different words, or ask a different AI tool. If the two answers disagree, that's your sign to slow down and check a real source. 
 When to skip the AI completely 
 For medical, legal and money decisions, use the AI to help you understand the topic and write your questions. Then take those questions to an actual doctor, lawyer or professional. 
 I turned these checks into a one-page printable you can keep by your desk. The  AI Fact-Check Cheat Sheet  is $3 on my Gumroad page.  AI tools ChatGPT Fact-checking

title: How to find and cancel the subscriptions you forgot about
dek: A 30-minute check that finds the $9.99 charges hiding in your bank statement, plus a free checklist to run it.
text:
I ran this check on our own accounts and found charges I'd stopped thinking about months ago. A free trial that turned into a paid plan. An app I used once. A streaming service we watched for one show. 
 None of them were big. Together they added up to real money every month. Here's the exact check I use, start to finish, in about 30 minutes. 
 Step 1: Pull three months of statements 
 One month isn't enough. Some subscriptions bill every three months or once a year, and those are the ones that sneak past you. Grab the last three months from: 
 
 Every bank account you use 
 Every credit card, including the store card in the junk drawer 
 PayPal, Apple, Google Play and Amazon, since they bill on their own 
 
 Step 2: Highlight anything that repeats 
 Go line by line and mark every charge that shows up more than once, even if the amount changes a little. Watch for odd names. A lot of companies bill under a parent company name you won't recognize at first. 
 
  Quick test for a strange charge  
 Search the exact name on your statement plus the word "charge." Someone else has almost always asked what it is. 
 
 Step 3: Sort each one into keep, cancel or downgrade 
 Ask one question for each: "Did I use this in the last 30 days?" If the answer is no, it goes on the cancel list. If you use it but not much, check for a cheaper plan or an ad-supported tier. 
 Step 4: Cancel the right way 
 
 Cancel inside the account settings, not by deleting the app. Deleting the app does not stop the bill. 
 Take a screenshot of the cancellation confirmation. 
 For anything billed through your phone, cancel in the App Store or Google Play subscriptions page. 
 Set a reminder to check your next statement and make sure the charge stopped. 
 
 Step 5: Stop it from happening again 
 When you start a free trial, put the end date in your phone calendar the same minute you sign up. That one habit catches most of these before they ever charge you. 
 I made a free printable checklist and Excel tracker that walks you through all five steps. You can grab the  Subscription Audit Checklist here , no cost.  Subscriptions Saving money Free checklist

title: How to get a contractor license in Minnesota (step by step)
dek: Minnesota has no "general contractor license." Here's which license you actually need, what's on the exam, and the deadlines that cost contractors money.
text:
You're good at the work. Homeowners keep asking if you can take the whole job. But the second you look up how to get licensed in Minnesota, you land on a state website full of forms, codes and statute numbers. 
 I help run a family framing and contracting business here in Minnesota, so I've been through this maze. Here's the plain-words version. 
 First: Minnesota doesn't have a "general contractor license" 
 This trips up almost everyone. What Minnesota has is a  residential building contractor license , issued by the Department of Labor and Industry (DLI). There are also two smaller versions: 
   License  What it lets you do  
  Residential building contractor (BC)  Everything, including new homes and detached garages  
  Residential remodeler (CR)  Work on existing homes only  
  Residential roofer (RR)  Roofing only (not gutters, soffit or fascia)   
 Commercial work is different. It's handled by local cities, not the state. 
 Do you even need a license? 
 Generally, yes, if you contract  directly with a homeowner  on a home with one to four units, and the job covers  more than one skill area  (say, framing plus drywall plus trim). 
 If you only work as a sub for a licensed contractor, you usually don't need your own license. There's also an exemption for very small operations. Check DLI's certificate of exemption to see if you qualify. 
 Why it matters: doing unlicensed work when you need a license is a misdemeanor in Minnesota, and cities can't issue you a building permit without one. 
 The 10 steps to getting licensed 
 
  Pick your business structure and name.  In Minnesota, the  business  gets licensed, not you personally. 
  File with the state and get your tax numbers.  
  Choose your qualifying person,  the owner or manager who takes the exam for the business. 
  Pass the exam.  More on this below. 
  Get insured.  General liability of at least $100,000 per occurrence and $300,000 total for bodily injury, plus $25,000 for property damage (or a $300,000 single-limit policy). 
  Apply for the license  through DLI. 
  Write bids and contracts that follow Minnesota law.  Everything in writing, including change orders. 
  Protect your pay with lien notices.  
  Hire subs and employees the right way,  including workers' comp. 
  Renew and keep up your continuing education:  14 hours every two-year license period. 
 
 What's on the Minnesota contractor exam? 
 
  110 multiple-choice questions  
  5.5 hours  to finish, and  70%  to pass 
 About  60% building code , and the rest on Minnesota laws and rules 
 No experience or school required to sit for it 
 
 They hand you the code book and a reference manual during the test. But 110 questions in 5.5 hours is about 3 minutes each. If you have to hunt for every answer, you'll run out of time. The people who pass know the most-tested numbers cold and know which chapter holds everything else. 
 If you fail, you wait  30 days  and submit a new application and fee. 
 The deadline that costs contractors the most money 
 It's the  pre-lien notice.  If you contract directly with a homeowner, the notice has to be in your written contract. With no written contract, you deliver it separately within  10 days  after the work is agreed on. Miss it, and you can lose your lien rights. 
 If a client won't pay, you generally have  120 days  after your last day of work to record a lien. 
 I keep a full step-by-step playbook with an exam study guide on my  Gumroad page  if you want everything in one place. 
 General information, not legal advice. Rules change, so confirm with the Minnesota Department of Labor and Industry before you apply. Checked November 2026.  Contractor license Minnesota Exam

title: How to start a house cleaning business during school hours
dek: Price your first job and book clients around school pickup.
text:
You don't need a free week to start a cleaning business. You need the hours between school drop-off and pickup, one honest price, and a first client who tells a friend. 
 Start with the schedule you actually have. If drop-off is 8:00 and pickup is 3:00, your work window is about 8:30 to 2:30 once you count driving. That's one bigger clean or two small ones a day, and that's enough to start. Quote from that real window, not from the day you wish you had. 
 Price the first job without guessing 
 Walk the house once, count the rooms that get cleaned every visit, and time yourself honestly on your own house first. A simple worked example: 
 
  A 3-bedroom, 2-bath home, cleaned every two weeks  
 Your timed pace says about 2.5 hours, inside the school window. 
 Quoted flat at $145: a number you can say out loud without flinching. 
 
 The tool I build my bids with lives on my  Gumroad page , linked from the icons at the top of this site. 
 Book the second client before the first clean 
 Ask the first client one question at booking: "Who on your street hates cleaning?" One name is worth more than any ad. Send that person one short text the same day, while your name is still fresh.  Cleaning business School hours Pricing
